biography.background: Third-generation oil and gas executive from Chambers County. Self-described Christian nationalist/MAGA conservative. Ranked among the most conservative members of the Texas Legislature in every session. Declines state salary and state health/pension benefits, donating his salary to local charities. Chaired the Texas House Freedom Caucus and has been the primary legislative engine for most significant Texas culture-war bills (transgender bathroom ban, vaccine mandate ban, school prayer, anti-ESG, women's sports ban) since 2019.

keyVotes.bill: SB 7 (88th Leg.) — COVID vaccine mandate ban for private employers including healthcare facilities
keyVotes.notes: Middleton's bill. Applied to all private employers including hospitals and clinics; no healthcare worker exception. Final vote 17-11 in Senate. He stated: 'This is about protecting the individual's ability [to stay employed] and making sure that they have the right to choose whether or not to get the shot.' Described by campaign as 'strongest ban on COVID vaccine mandates in the country.'

keyVotes.bill: SB 8 (89th Leg.) — Women's Privacy Act (transgender bathroom ban in schools, government buildings)
keyVotes.notes: Middleton primary sponsor. Called it 'the strongest Women's Privacy Act in America.' Bars transgender individuals from bathrooms/changing rooms matching gender identity in schools and government-owned buildings.

keyVotes.bill: SB 406 (89th Leg.) — Birth certificates must list biological sex; minors prohibited from changing sex marker
keyVotes.notes: Passed 20-11 on party-line Senate vote.

keyVotes.bill: HB 229 (89th Leg.) — Women's Bill of Rights (state records must reflect biological sex at birth)
keyVotes.notes: Authored by Rep. Ellen Troxclair; Middleton carried in Senate. Birth certificates and driver's licenses must reflect biological sex.

keyVotes.bill: SB 763 (88th Leg.) — Chaplains in public schools (may replace school counselors)
keyVotes.notes: Allows school districts to employ paid or volunteer chaplains without requiring counseling certification or training. Final passage via conference committee report.

keyVotes.bill: SB 11 (89th Leg.) — School prayer and Bible reading period in public schools
keyVotes.notes: Establishes optional prayer and Bible/religious text reading periods in public K-12 and charter schools. Requires parent/employee written consent. Passed House 88-48. Middleton stated 'there's no such thing as separation of church and state' when challenged on constitutionality. Signed by governor; effective September 1, 2025.

keyVotes.bill: SB 176 / SB 8 (88th Leg.) — Universal ESA (Education Savings Account) voucher bill
keyVotes.notes: Middleton filed SB 176 for universal ESA program. Voted YES on the broader ESA bill in 88th and 89th Legislatures. Strong school choice advocate.

keyVotes.bill: ESA bill (89th Leg.) — School voucher program
keyVotes.notes: Voted YES on establishing ESA program. Argued private schools would open specifically to serve special education students.

keyVotes.bill: Texas Senate anti-ESG legislation (SB 13 / SB 19 prior sessions, related bills)
keyVotes.notes: Middleton described as having 'led the charge against radical woke policies like DEI, ESG, Critical Race Theory.' SB 13 banned state business with banks using ESG policies on fossil fuels; SB 19 prohibited business with companies supporting gun safety policies. (Note: SB 13 subsequently ruled unconstitutional by federal court in Feb. 2026 on First Amendment grounds.)

keyVotes.bill: SB 6 / SB 7 (89th Leg.) — Energy grid reliability; incentivize dispatchable thermal generation
keyVotes.notes: Middleton publicly backed SB 6/7, stating: 'In a distorted market with intermittent, renewable technologies receiving an unfair advantage through heavy tax subsidies, there is a need to incentivize new, reliable, dispatchable generation ... I support any legislation that assists in putting new steel in the ground for dispatchable, reliable generation.' Explicitly frames renewables as 'intermittent' market distortion.

keyVotes.bill: SB 12 (88th Leg.) — Ban on taxpayer-funded lobbying by local governments
keyVotes.notes: Also filed SB 19 (ban taxpayer lobbying by local entities, passed). Recognized as Taxpayer Champion by Texans for Fiscal Responsibility.

keyVotes.bill: Save Women's Sports Act (88th Leg.) — Ban transgender women/girls from collegiate women's sports
keyVotes.notes: Passed. Campaign describes as cornerstone achievement.

keyVotes.bill: Texas omnibus abortion restriction bills — SB 8 (6-week ban), Senate abortion bills
keyVotes.notes: Voted to pass 6-week abortion ban with citizen-enforcement mechanism. Also voted for criminal penalties for providers. Cosponsored abortion drug reporting requirements. Sponsored perinatal palliative care bill banning third-trimester abortions except medical emergency.

keyVotes.bill: Texas Senate abortion ban exception clarification — SB 31 (Life of the Mother Act)
keyVotes.notes: Voted for SB 31 which clarifies that Texas law allows medically necessary care for pregnant women (part of post-Dobbs technical fix). Texas Alliance for Life scored this as pro-life.

keyVotes.bill: Property tax cuts (SB 4 — homestead exemption $100K to $140K; SB 23 — up to $200K)
keyVotes.notes: Supported property tax relief measures. Voted for $336B bipartisan budget that included $32B property tax relief (31-0 Senate vote, 2025).

keyVotes.bill: Gun/firearms — SB 755 (firearms sales tax holiday) and gun privacy bill (HB 1403 companion)
keyVotes.notes: SB 755: annual sales tax holiday for firearms, accessories, ammunition. HB 1403 companion: prohibits child placement/state agencies from requiring foster parents to disclose specific firearms kept in home. Worked with NRA on State Fair of Texas gun ban clarification.

keyVotes.bill: Conference Committee on SB 15 (89th Leg.) — Housing supply reform (townhomes/starter homes by-right in large cities)
keyVotes.notes: Middleton served on conference committee for SB 15, Lt. Gov. Patrick's priority housing supply bill. Bill allows townhomes and starter homes by-right in cities >150K in counties >300K. Not a primary author; role limited to conference committee. Insufficient evidence to score this axis definitively on its own.

keyVotes.bill: SB 854 — Religious organizations developing multi-family housing on vacant land
keyVotes.notes: Would limit cities' authority to restrict religious organizations from developing multi-family housing on vacant land. Narrow supply-side measure.

keyVotes.bill: 'Integrity 7' election package — Voter roll integrity and election procedures
keyVotes.notes: Joint authored package with Senators Creighton, Huffman, Kolkhorst, Paxton, Perry, and Parker. Aimed at voter roll maintenance and election procedures.

keyVotes.bill: SB 476 (89th Leg.) — Increased punishment for intoxication manslaughter with court-ordered interlock device
keyVotes.notes: Harsher sentencing bill — if someone violated court-ordered interlock device and caused intoxication manslaughter, increases punishment level. Consistent with punishment/deterrence approach.

businessBackground.description: Independent oil and gas company operating 60+ wells in South Texas and along the Gulf Coast. Also runs ranching, cattle, and farming operations in Chambers, Jefferson, Kimble, Liberty, and Webb Counties.
businessBackground.relevance: Direct financial interest in fossil fuel industry. Explicit legislative advocacy for dispatchable thermal generation and against renewables subsidies. Anti-ESG legislation directly benefits his industry. Self-funded campaign ($11M+ raised, $5M+ cash on hand per user brief) from personal/business wealth.
businessBackground.conflictNotes: As AG, would have authority to enforce/oppose environmental regulations affecting oil and gas industry. His energy policy positions are fully aligned with his business interests.

positionConflicts.conflict: iVoterGuide responses appear to contain contradictory answers — one suggesting Medicaid/Medicare should remain available, another suggesting they should be defunded. Most likely reflects different survey formats or question framing. Scored conservatively based on campaign's actual emphasis (no stated expansion; consistent with anti-government-healthcare posture).

Legislation Middleton championed (anti-ESG fossil fuel boycott ban) was ruled unconstitutional by federal court in Feb. 2026 on First Amendment grounds. No response from Middleton campaign found. Doesn't change the underlying policy position, but relevant context for AG candidacy (he touted championing this law as a feature).

evidenceSummary.notes: Middleton has an unusually well-documented legislative record for a state-level candidate: 7 years across House and Senate, dozens of authored bills, multiple scorecards from ideological organizations, and extensive media coverage. The gaps are primarily in housing/transit (not a focus of his work) and policing/criminal justice (limited beyond DWI sentencing and anti-crime rhetoric). His policy positions are internally consistent and extreme-right on virtually every axis covered. The record is more extensive and confirmatory than most state legislative candidates.
